endorsements.quote: The reuse of training data as test data, so-called “data leakage”, can artificially inflate performance estimates on the test set20, and cross-validation on the same cohort is suboptimal.
Panelists strongly agreed (92.86%, statementfive) that clinicians should be educated on the intended use-case, limitations and interpretation of a tool 33.

Maintaining clinical skills alongside AI adoption is essential, as deskilling due to increased reliance on AI can undermine a clinician’s ability to question algorithmic outputs or recognize when model errors may have occurred59–61.

The panel emphasized that neuroimaging AI tools are not intended to function as a standalone, automated diagnostic tool but rather to enhance clinician confidence in decision-making, and that outputs should be interpreted in line with other test results.
Prior to sharing, neuroimaging data should be deidentified by removing the patient’s name, geographic location, and other sensitive health information47,48.

unlisted_practices: Train and validate neuroimaging AI on completely independent cohorts that are diverse and representative.
Evaluate neuroimaging AI with sensitivity, specificity, and AUC, choosing metrics according to intended clinical use.
Involve dementia clinicians, AI experts, imaging experts, radiologists, and patients early in the design of neuroimaging AI tools.
Evaluate the cost-effectiveness of AI tools in memory clinics to inform resource allocation.
Provide continuous updates, maintenance, and dedicated personnel for AI tools after integration to maintain robustness amid data shifts.
Update computational infrastructure and hire technical staff to support large-scale AI adoption.
Use federated learning with privacy-enhancing measures such as differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, and homomorphic encryption to protect patient data.
Establish transparent governance frameworks with clear consent procedures, oversight mechanisms, and policies for public-private data collaborations.
Include data-sharing clauses in consent forms for neuroimaging studies.
Localize AI tools, including translation of interfaces, outputs, and clinical reports, for multilingual and low-resource settings.

screen.reason: Expert Delphi consensus guidelines and recommendations on the design, implementation, ethics, and quality for AI neuroimaging tools in memory clinics.
